implementation_notes: The framework owns both roles: an @Injectable() class implementing NestInterceptor receives an ExecutionContext (the Context) and a CallHandler, and calling next.handle() - which returns an Observable - continues to the route handler; returning a different Observable without calling handle() replaces the handler entirely, which is how caching or stubbed responses are implemented. Binding is scope-selective through @UseInterceptors (controller/method) or APP_INTERCEPTOR for global registration, and dependency injection supplies collaborators. The classic Dispatcher is the Nest runtime and the classic abstract Interceptor is the typed interface plus decorator; Angular shows the same pattern for HTTP with plain functions instead of classes.
pitfalls: Not calling next.handle() disables the route handler for that scope - deliberate for caching, but it also disables every interceptor bound after this one.

Order follows binding scope (global -> controller -> method) and the declared order inside each level; there is no priority keyword, so a wrongly scoped interceptor silently runs before the guard it assumed had already run.
Interceptors registered with useGlobalInterceptors() outside any module cannot inject dependencies (no module context) - register them through APP_INTERCEPTOR instead.
RxJS semantics leak into the chain: a catchError that swallows an error prevents later operators from seeing it, and a missing handle() call leaves the request without a response stream.

variants.name: Angular functional HTTP interceptors
variants.implementation_notes: Angular's recommendation is the functional form: an interceptor is a function (req: HttpRequest<unknown>, next: HttpHandlerFn) => Observable<HttpEvent<unknown>>, registered declaratively with provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([...])), where the order in the array is the chain order. Because HttpRequest/HttpResponse are immutable, an interceptor modifies a request by cloning it (req.clone({...})) - which also makes retries idempotent - and per-request metadata travels in the typed HttpContext map (HttpContextToken) instead of ad-hoc headers. The class-based HttpInterceptor + HTTP_INTERCEPTORS form is the legacy variant; the classic Dispatcher is Angular's HttpClient and the classic Interceptor role is the function signature.
pitfalls: Requests are immutable: mutating req.headers directly does nothing (or throws in strict mode) and the change is silently lost - always clone.
Interceptors only see requests made through HttpClient; calls made with fetch/axios bypass the chain entirely, so a security header added here can be missing elsewhere.
The response stream can emit several events, so an interceptor must filter on the terminal event (HttpEventType.Response) before acting on a body.

Injecting dependencies works because functional interceptors run in the injection context of the registering injector - capturing services at module scope (outside the function) fails or binds to the wrong injector.
